lines: Your vowels are from Thessaloniki, Sophia. I'd stake my register on it, so tell me which part.
Ano Poli, up by the walls. My mother taught literature at the school there.
Then you walked past my father's funeral home every day of your childhood. I'd have nodded to you on the stairs.
The one on the hill with the heavy door? I was terrified of that door until I was twelve.
Stelios, your wife's name is Despina, isn't it? At the old library?
It is, and she stamped every book in that building herself.
She stamped mine, every Saturday for six years. She let me take four when the rule was three.
That sounds exactly like her. She always said the rules were for people who didn't read, and I'd like her to know you remember.
I keep the register in Greek as well as Common. Would you check my spelling? The dead deserve their accents in the right place.
I'd be honoured. I'll also correct your handwriting, I'm afraid, it's a funeral director's scrawl.
Funeral directors write beautifully, Sophia, we just do it in a hurry.
My father had started losing people, before all this. He still knew me, mostly, and I hold on to the mostly.
I've sat with a great many families holding on to a mostly. It isn't a small thing to hold, and some days it's the whole of it.
Thank you. You put that exactly right, and I've listened to the best speakers in Europe.
Nineteen years of practice, and a city that taught us both to talk slowly.
Suit check, Taras. I know you've done it, and I'm doing it anyway.
Every morning, and you've never once found anything wrong.
That's how you know it's working.
Kashtan, sit, the man's doing his job. He'll check you next, and you'll like it.
My tourists used to ask if Chernobyl could happen again, Wes. I'd tell them only if people stop being careful.
Hanford had folks saying it'll be fine for fifty years. We spent twenty cleaning up after them.
So it's the same job, you and me, from two ends. Somebody makes the mess, and we count the heads.
Copy that, it's the same job.
The mule's started following Kashtan around when I'm on shift.
Kashtan's very proud of it. He's never had a mule before.
Me neither, to be fair. I didn't ask for this one.
Nobody asks for the good things here, Wes. They just turn up and eat your apples.
My father was a liquidator in 1986. He went in so the rest of us wouldn't have to.
My dad fitted pipe at Hanford his whole life. He never said much about what was in them.
Then we both grew up next to something nobody would talk about. Maybe that's why we keep the fence.
Could be, Taras. Somebody's got to stand at it who knows what's on the other side.
You cook, my friend? I can smell it on you, onion and paprika.
I don't cook, I make beans. And you smell like somebody who burns meat and calls it a skill.
Burns, you say? Che, I ran a grill for twelve years.
Then you've been burning things for twelve years, bre, and well done.
I tried your asado last night, Argentine. It needed salt.
It needed nothing! You put salt on everything, your tongue is broken.
My tongue fed forty regulars every night in Novi Sad, and none of them complained.
Because they were afraid of you, che! I've seen your face.
Okay, I'll say it once, and if you tell anybody I'll deny it. Your beans are good, Vuk.
Just good, is it? They're the best beans in Serbia.
They're good, that's all. Mine would be better, if I made beans, which I don't, because I've got standards.
Ha, so eat another bowl and say that again, bre.
Your meat and my beans, on the same night, at one fire. People would come from three zones.
A cook-off, my friend? You'd lose, and you'd lose in front of everybody.
Not a cook-off. One table, both of us at it, and nobody leaves hungry.
Now that, che, I would come to. I might even sit down at it.
My grandmother always said people who argue about food are the only honest ones, Vuk.
Uncle Dragan would have thrown you out of his kitchen for touching his pot, and then fed you.
That's the same thing, my friend. That's exactly the same thing.
Allora, a Cuban! I had a Cuban regular once who drank mojitos at seven in the morning, and I never judged him.
Perfect, then I'll do the conversation for both of us, dai.
That's what I was afraid of.
You know what you need, Osvaldo? A bar with a little stage, and a band on a Thursday.
Every bar needs music! I'd keep a corner for you, and I wouldn't talk through it, I promise.
You'd talk through it, asere. You'd talk through your own funeral.
You stopped talking for a whole minute in that fight, and I noticed.
I was concentrating! It happens, rarely, but it happens.
Don't do it again. It was strange, and I didn't like it.
Mamma mia, he likes my talking! I knew it, I always know.
I said I didn't like the quiet, asere, and that's different.
I rate everything out of ten, you know that. Your fire's a nine, Osvaldo.
Nobody gets a ten. Not my coffee, not my wife's cooking, not even me.
Then I'll take the nine. It's better than the hotel manager ever gave me.
You talk so nobody hears what you don't say, Gianluca. I know, because I keep quiet for the same reason.
You're a dangerous man, you know that? Sitting there quietly, noticing everything.
Sit with me a while. You don't have to say it, I just want you to know I heard it.
Your accent's Achrafieh, habibi. Don't tell me, near the sea, below Sassine?
Two streets from the clinic on the hill, the one by the church. Ten years drawing blood there.
I've driven up that hill a thousand times with the siren on! I probably brought you half your patients.
Then you're the reason my Tuesdays were so busy. I always wondered who to blame.
You heal with fel, Ziad, and I heal with blood. Our mothers would want a word with both of us.
Mine would ask if it's working. It's working, so she'd make coffee and stop asking.
Mine would make coffee too, and then ask anyway, all afternoon.
That's an Achrafieh mother. They never stop asking, and they're always right.
You're slower than me and you're still always on time, Elie. How do you manage it?
I talk the whole way through. The patient forgets to panic, and when nobody panics, nothing goes wrong.
I just run, faster than the panic, every time.
And who catches you when you trip, habibi?
The port, Ziad. I was at the clinic that day, and people came in for hours, cut by the glass, and I kept thinking about whoever was out there choosing.
That was us, me and three vans. I don't talk about it.
You don't have to. I just wanted you to know somebody at the other end was catching them.
Thank you, habibi. I always wondered if anyone was.
You walk like the Quartieri, ragazzo. Which street was yours?
Two streets above Via Toledo, over my mother's tabaccheria.
The tabaccheria was Rosaria's? I changed her lock twice, and she argued about the price both times.
That sounds like her. So you're the locksmith with the door that was always open, the one every mother sent for.
The thing in your arm, Enzo. I don't like it, and I'll say so once, because I knew your mother.
It didn't lie about the price, Marco. That's more than the Scarlets ever did.
A thing that tells you the price honestly is still selling you something.
Then I bought it, and I'll pay for it. And don't worry about my mother, she'd have shouted at it too.
You hold the line the way the old men held the bus stop on Via Toledo. Nobody gets past you.
Thirty years of standing in doorways, ragazzo. It's the same thing.
My coach used to say the feet tell you everything, and yours never move.
They move when they need to. Most of the time, they don't need to.
You coached the little ones on Saturdays. Your mother told me while I was fixing her lock, and she was prouder of that than of the medals.
She never said that to me. She shouted at the referees, mostly.
Mothers in the Quartieri tell the locksmith, Enzo, never the son. That's how it works.
Then thank you for telling me. I'd have gone my whole life not knowing.
Fourth, twice, Marco. Do you know what it is, being nearly good enough?
I know how it feels to be sixty-three and frightened of a piece of paper. Maybe that's worse, or maybe it's the same.
You, frightened of something? I don't believe it.
Believe it, ragazzo. Nobody carries a thing like that well alone, so let's not.
That accent's Łódź, girl. I'd know it anywhere.
Widzew, by the stadium. And you're from the old factory side of town, I can hear the looms in it.
Nineteen years at a clothing plant, fixing forty sewing machines.
And I spent eight years answering phones for an insurer two tram stops away. We probably rode the same tram for a decade.
The six o'clock tram, with everybody asleep standing up. I'd have been the one with grease on her sleeve.
Did they ever call you by your surname at the plant, Marta?
Never once, in nineteen years. It was just Marta, come quickly, line four's stopped.
Same at the call centre. First name on the badge, so the callers could shout it properly.
Then we'll use each other's surnames here, Nowak, and see how it feels.
It feels very strange, Kowalska. I think I like it.
You tore the symbols off those robes yourself, didn't you? You did it badly, so give them here, and I'll stitch the holes.
My mother sewed shirts for thirty years, and I started on the line at nineteen. Of course I can sew.
Then stitch them so nobody can tell what was there. I'd be grateful, and I don't say that often.
I said yes to the Cult for my grandmother as well as for me, Marta. We were starving, and she was sick.
In the first winter, people did what they had to. I'm not going to stand here and judge a woman from Łódź for keeping her babcia fed.
Most people never fixed a machine at dawn with a manager screaming at them. We both know how it feels to do the job in front of you.
Heliopolis, ya basha? I can hear it in your vowels.
Heliopolis, yes, a flat I could still draw from memory. And you're Shubra, I'd bet a well on it.
Shubra, born and raised, and my father's van was in every street of it. Gamal Pest Control, since 1987.
The van with the big painted cockroach? Everybody in Cairo knew that van.
My father painted it himself, and he was very proud of it, and the cockroach was very ugly.
Have you eaten, Sherif? You look like a man who forgets, down in that hive.
I eat koshari in my head every day, ya basha. It doesn't fill you, but it helps.
Then come to the spring at Splintertree, and I'll make the real thing, or as near as the orcs' lentils allow.
Durotar lentils in a koshari? My mother would cry. I'll be there tomorrow.
Your water's the cleanest I've had since I got here, Tarek. I catalogued it, and it's a very boring sample.
Boring is the best thing anyone's ever said about my water.
In my trade, boring means nothing's living in it. I think it's the same in yours.
It's exactly the same. You'd have made a good engineer.
And you'd have made a terrible pest controller, you'd want to fix the cockroaches.
I'll tell you plainly, Sherif, because you're from home and I want somebody from home to know. I left Cairo inside a week because of a man I loved.
Ya Tarek, my friend. And you've carried that by yourself all this time?
Here nobody asks me questions I'd have to lie about. But I wanted to say it in our accent, once.
Then you've said it, and I've heard it, and you're still my friend from home. Next time, you eat at mine.
You're mapping the sky too! I've seen your charts at the Moonglade post, the northern ones.
Then you've also seen that yours have the eastern cluster in the wrong place.
Wrong, you say? Ay, no, I checked it eleven nights in a row!
From a lake. I checked it from a ridge in Felwood, lying in the snow, for a month.
I went back and checked your cluster, Astrid. You were wrong, and I was a little bit wrong too.
A little bit wrong is still wrong. But I'll accept a little bit.
Then we split it, po. My lake and your ridge, and we'd have the whole thing.
I work alone. I've always worked alone.
So did I, until a minibus full of tourists. You get used to company, I promise.
Where you're from, which way did you look first, every night?
South, always south, for the Cross. I found it first for every tour, every single time.
I looked north, for the lights. It seems we spent our whole lives with our backs to each other.
And then we both had to learn this sky from nothing. That's funny, Astrid, you have to admit.
It's a little funny. I'll admit a little.
I laid your charts and mine side by side last night, and they fit, Astrid. They actually fit.
I know they do. I did the same thing on Tuesday and didn't tell you.
Because you'd do exactly this, and I wanted one more quiet day first.
You cry when people see the stars for the first time. I almost never cry, and I've always envied people who can.
It's not a weakness, it's just what my face does when something's too big.
Then come up to my ridge one clear night. I'll lie in the snow, and you can do the crying for both of us.
Deal, but you're bringing the blanket. Chileans aren't made for snow.
You cut runes too, maestro! Qué más, show me your line work.
I don't cut them to be looked at. I cut them so they hold.
Every line's there to be looked at, parce, that's half of why it holds.
That's a tattooist's opinion. It isn't wrong, but it's loud.
Your rune on the gate yesterday. The third stroke was hurried.
It glowed, though! Bright as a sign in Laureles.
It glowed, and it will fail in a month, and someone will be standing next to it when it does.
Ay, okay, okay. Show me how you'd do it, then, and slowly, I'm watching.
Eleven years before your master praised you once? Parce, I'd have quit in a week.
You'd have quit in a day. Then you'd have come back, because the work mattered more than your pride.
How can you possibly know that?
Because you came back to the gate this morning and cut the rune again. I saw you.
You were watching? Qué pena, it was six in the morning.
Your new rune on the gate will hold.
Wait, maestro, was that praise? That sounded like praise!
It was an observation. Please don't tattoo it on anything.
Too late, parce, it's going on my arm.
Maestro, my little brother. I paid for his school, and I never once told him I was proud of him.
My master never told me either, not for eleven years. I learned it from how he corrected me.
I think a brother who paid for the school said it every month, in the only way that counted.
Another one with green eyes! Habibi, how did you pay for yours?
Carefully, after a week of consideration, with my eyes open. How did you pay for yours?
In about four seconds, in a jungle full of wounded people.
Then one of us chose and one of us reacted. I'll let you decide which.
Your arithmetic's wrong, Karim. You took it to be useful, and I took it to save the fifth patient, and that's different.
It's the same sum written in a different order. Useful is saving people with the sentiment taken out.
Don't take the sentiment out, it's the only part that hurts. The hurting's the point.
That's precisely why I took it out.
I surveyed the desert east of Amman for fifteen years. Out there you learn a line's only as honest as the person who drew it.
And in an ambulance you learn the line moves every time somebody screams.
Then we'd both have hated each other's jobs.
Probably, but I'd have liked you in the van. You'd have kept the count straight.
Okay, I'll say it, you're the only one who argues the fel with me properly. Everybody else just looks sad.
I'm tired of people being sad on my behalf. I imagine you are too.
I'm exhausted, habibi. Let's keep arguing, it's restful.
When you chose, at the port, did you ever choose wrong?
Never once, and I carry every one of them anyway. Being right doesn't make it light.
I always believed that if the sum was right, the weight went away. I'm less sure of that than I used to be.
It doesn't go away, it just gets carried by more people. Sit with me, and we'll split it.
You're a musician, aren't you? You hold your hands like they're still holding something.
Trumpet, sixteen years. Don't ask me to play.
I wasn't going to. I'd only criticise, and you'd hate me.
Second violin, I'd guess. You've got the face of somebody who's been told off by a conductor.
Eleven years, by a man with a stick. You're annoyingly right.
You hummed the Bartók again last night. You were flat on the fourth bar.
I wasn't flat, I was expressive, which you'd know if you'd ever played anything but hotel jazz.
Hotel jazz paid my rent for sixteen years, and the tourists talked through all of it.
At least they talked through something good. Mine coughed through Brahms.
I want an ensemble, Osvaldo, not an audience. Three or four people who can hold a line.
I know what you want. Don't ask me to play for you.
I'm asking you to listen and tell me when I'm wrong, because you'd actually know.
That, I can do. You'll hate it.
I'll hate it and I'll be better for it, which is the whole point of anybody who's any good.
My brother plays piano better than me. We fought every night and played every night.
That's the only way to make music worth hearing. Comfortable ensembles are boring.
You'd like him. He's rude, like you.
I was unbearable for two years here. I knew I was doing it, and I did it anyway.
I burned ships for the Bloodsail and didn't care whose. Don't tell me about unbearable.
Then neither of us is allowed to be smug about the other.
Fine, we'll just be rude, like musicians.
You're from Brisbane? Mate, I told everyone not to say Queensland, and here you are.
Sorry, no worries, I'll keep it quiet. You're Victoria, by the sound of it, all that cold made you serious.
Ballarat, and I'm not serious, I'm careful. There's a difference, and you don't know it.
I've been bitten by a taipan, Skye. I know heaps about careful, mostly what happens when you're not.
You stuck your hand in that nest without looking, Callum. I watched you.
I looked, I just looked fast. The spider was more scared of me, mate.
The spider wasn't scared of anything, it was the size of a dinner plate!
And now it's my mate. You're welcome to come and meet it.
Not a chance, and if you get bitten I'm not carrying you.
You were a vet nurse, weren't you? You held that wolf's paw like you were checking for a break.
Years of other people's dogs and cats, and a lot of farm visits. Why do you ask?
I had a blue heeler, Biscuit. Best mate I ever had, and I had to leave her behind.
Oh, mate, I'm sorry. Heelers are the best dogs going, and they know it.
Righto, here's the deal. You look before you put your hand in things, and I'll stop yelling about it.
That's a terrible deal for you, you love yelling about it.
I do, but I'd rather you didn't die. Have we got a deal?
I'm better with animals than people, Skye. Always have been, and I didn't notice till here.
You're all right with this person, mate, and I've noticed.
Yeah, you reckon? Then I reckon I'm getting better at it.
You're getting there. I'll keep yelling at you till you're perfect.
You're a coach, I can see it from here! You stand like you're about to blow a whistle.
Under-sixteen camogie, and you're one too, so. Nobody walks like that unless they've done a thousand warm-ups.
Pelota, and PE for the whole school! Race you to the top of the hill, right now!
You're on, and I'll be waiting for you at the top.
That was a dead heat on the hill, Iker, and I want a rematch.
I won by a step! I keep score of everything, and it was a step.
You keep score of everything? So do I, and I've got you down as losing.
Then we're both liars, and we race again tomorrow at seven!
You shout at people until they get better. Where did you learn that?
My first coach, a nun with a whistle and no mercy. Who taught you?
My grandfather, on the fronton, in his txapela, shouting louder than the sea.
Then we were both raised by maniacs, and look how well we turned out.
If we ever put a team together out here, Iker, I'm captain.
You think you're captain? No, I'm the captain! Fine, we'll be co-captains, and we'll shout in turns.
Nobody'll be able to hear a thing, and the team'll be brilliant.
Ninety names, Saoirse. I've got them all in my pocket, and I don't talk about it, because if I start I'll stop shouting.
I've names of my own I'm still looking for. Eleven girls in a minibus, and I was the one driving it.
I know it well. You keep shouting, and I'll keep shouting, and if either of us goes quiet, the other one notices.
You're a sailor, mali. I can tell by how you watch the horizon.
Sailing instructor, on the Hardangerfjord. Teenagers and dinghies, mostly.
Car ferries, me, out of Split, fifteen years. Two hundred passengers and a crew of eight.
Then you'd have hated my dinghies. They capsize if you look at them.
Everything capsizes if you look at it wrong. That's the first thing the sea teaches you.
Luka, the first storm you called, did it go the way you wanted?
It nearly drowned me, and that's how I knew it was mine.
Mine knocked over a barn with people in it. A girl broke her leg.
Then you know the weight, and you'll call it carefully. Careful is what keeps the passengers alive.
You make the fire every morning before anybody's up. My mate on the Marjan did the same with the coffee.
Somebody has to do it. It's a good hour, the first one.
You're right, mali. Wake me next time, and I'll keep you company and not talk.
You'll talk, Luka. Dalmatians always talk.
Only a little, and only about the weather.
When the wind's bad, I'd like you on deck with me. I trust you to tell me when to stop.
And I'll trust you to stop when I tell you. That's how a crew works.
Then that's what we are, I think, a crew of two.
A crew of two is how every good crossing starts.
